messages.body_plain:
STATISTICAL ECOLOGY STUDENTSHIP:   MIXED EFFECTS MODELS IN DISTANCE
SAMPLING

This PhD studentship will be within the National Centre for Statistical
Ecology (NCSE), a joint research centre between the Universities of
Kent, Cambridge and St Andrews, and will be based at St Andrews.

Nearly 200 countries signed up to the 2010 targets to reduce the rate of
loss of biodiversity.  This has generated a need to quantify regional
trends in abundance and biodiversity, and an increase in wildlife
monitoring surveys based on selecting sites within a region according to
a randomized design.  Generally, these sites are then treated as fixed,
but to allow inference to the wider region that they represent, it is
more appropriate to model site as a random effect.

Many monitoring surveys are conducted using distance sampling, which
encompasses several methods for estimating animal abundance
(http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.book/dist_encyc_env.pdf).
Researchers at St Andrews have been at the forefront of development of
distance sampling methods, authoring several books and the Distance
computer program, which is the industry standard for analysing distance
sampling surveys.

This project will explore the potential for mixed effects models in
distance sampling.  The main focus will be on the analysis of annual
regional surveys based on line or point transect sampling at
representative locations.  Models will be developed to quantify
spatially varying trends in abundance and detectability.

The successful candidate will join a large and thriving group of
research staff and students in the EPSRC-funded NCSE
(http://www.ncse.org.uk/), and will be located in the Centre for
Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
(http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/).  Supervisors will be Monique Mackenzie
(http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/monique/) and Stephen Buckland
(http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/stb/stb.html).

The studentship covers home fees and the enhanced research council
stipend for statistics students for 3 years.  It is open to any
applicant, but applicants from outside the European Union will need to
seek additional funding to cover the difference between home and
overseas fees.  Applicants should have a first degree in statistics, or
in a related discipline with a strong quantitative component.  Start
date: September 2008.

If you are interested in applying, please e-mail Monique Mackenzie
(mon...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk <mailto:mon...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk>) or Steve
Buckland (st...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk <mailto:st...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk>),
attaching a CV.  Closing date: May 30 2008.

messages.body_plain:
I have been using DISTANCE's survey design features and have a couple of
questions about projections.

1. Under File|Project properties|Geographic tab there is a "Parameter"
button under the "Maps and Geographic calculations" section of the
dialogue box where you can specify values for the false easting, false
northing, central meridian and standard parallel 1. Is the "Standard
Parallel 1" parameter the same as the "Scale" or "Latitude of Origin"
parameter used by ArcGIS/ArcMap?

2. I have imported a shapefile in a geographic coordinate system
(decimal degrees) into DISTANCE and projected it for the purpose of
distance calculations. For the same shapefile, ArcMap calculates the
polygon area as 628 sq. km using a Mercator projection but distance
calculates the "Stratum Area" as 773 sq. km. I am assuming the stratum
area is the same as the polygon area in which case why is there such a
big difference in the calculated area?

3. If I have projected a geographic coordinate shapefile with DISTANCE
for the purpose calculating distances, do the x-y coordinates generated
by line sampler automatically generate these values as unprojected
geographic coordinates?

Thanks for your help.

Winston

messages.body_plain:
Winston:

Hello again Winston; sounds like you're hard at work designing a survey
for your 'roos.  I'm weak on my GIS knowledge, but I'll give a whirl
with your questions.

Kay, Winston wrote:
> > I have been using DISTANCE's survey design features and have a couple of
> > questions about projections.
> >
> > 1. Under File|Project properties|Geographic tab there is a "Parameter"
> > button under the "Maps and Geographic calculations" section of the
> > dialogue box where you can specify values for the false easting, false
> > northing, central meridian and standard parallel 1. Is the "Standard
> > Parallel 1" parameter the same as the "Scale" or "Latitude of Origin"
> > parameter used by ArcGIS/ArcMap?
> >

No, it is not the case that standard parallel 1 is the same as scale or
latitude of origin.  Creep inside any "*.prj" file (can be opened with
Notepad), you will see each of the bits in the Geographic tab expressed
therein.

> > 2. I have imported a shapefile in a geographic coordinate system
> > (decimal degrees) into DISTANCE and projected it for the purpose of
> > distance calculations. For the same shapefile, ArcMap calculates the
> > polygon area as 628 sq. km using a Mercator projection but distance
> > calculates the "Stratum Area" as 773 sq. km. I am assuming the stratum
> > area is the same as the polygon area in which case why is there such a
> > big difference in the calculated area?
> >

Someone more knowledgeable on this subject will undoubtedly weigh in
here, but I think what you've described is area calculation taking place
in two different projections (ArcMap used a Mercator projection to
obtain the 773 figure), while Distance is using *unprojected* degrees to
compute the 628 figure.  That is the reason for projection, to make the
calculations you are describing comparable.

> > 3. If I have projected a geographic coordinate shapefile with DISTANCE
> > for the purpose calculating distances, do the x-y coordinates generated
> > by line sampler automatically generate these values as unprojected
> > geographic coordinates?
> >

The coordinates produced by the survey design engine will be in the same
projection as that of the shapefile used to describe the study area.
Take a look at Chapter 3 of the "Distance users guide" you will see an
example of designing a survey using the survey design engine, and you
will be greeted with the information "Note that the new samplers have
been added to the project as a new data layer, and this new data layer
has an associated GIS shapefile, so this may be a more convenient format
for exporting to other systems such as GPS.   "

messages.body_plain:
Members of this list may be interested in the following. The website
is really designed for 16-21 year olds so please forward details on
to any individuals/groups who might be interested.

Win The Dream Whale Sailing Trip of a Lifetime www.whalequest.org.uk <http://www.whalequest.org.uk>

Young conservationists with an interest in marine life are being
given the opportunity of a lifetime by researchers at the University
of St Andrews.

The University is offering the chance for a budding David
Attenboroughs to join them on a whale research project around
Madeira. The youngster will sail with scientists on a week-long trip
around Madeira on the International Fund for Animal Welfare's unique
vessel Song of the Whale.

The lucky winner of the competition will take part in the research
expedition aboard IFAW's state-of-the-art education and research
vessel, which was launched in 2004 by actor Pierce Brosnan.
Non-invasive studies carried out on the boat play an important role
in the conservation and protection of whales and other cetaceans.

The purpose of the September trip is to study the acoustic behaviour
of beaked whales in the Atlantic Ocean, and the young observer is
likely to catch sight of these rare animals and sperm whales.

A screenshot from the online game.
Young people aged between 16 and 21 who reside in the UK can take
part in the online competition, which is based on a scientific aerial
survey of whales. Participants must estimate the actual number of
whales present based on how many they spot during the course of the
game. The better their estimates, the higher their chance of winning,
and players can compare their results with those of professional
marine biologists. The competition closes on the 31st June and the
winner will be announced on the 7th July.

The idea of introducing youngsters to this scientific methodology is
part of a new drive to find the next generation of statisticians.
Since population estimation techniques are included in biology Higher
and A-level exams, the game has been designed as a useful learning
resource for 16 to 19-year-old students.

The innovative method of engaging young people in conservation issues
is the brainchild of St Andrews' researcher Dr David Borchers, who
has been working on the project for several years. A statistician who
specialises in analysing marine animal populations, Dr
Borchers  said: "Uncertainty is statisticians' bread and butter and
uncertainty is unavoidable when estimating wildlife population sizes
- which is why the next generation of conservationists will need to
be statistically literate.

"To conserve animal populations under threat, we need to know how
many remain and whether their numbers are increasing or decreasing.
But just finding out how many there are is often surprisingly
difficult - whales cannot be counted like humans - instead, we have
to estimate numbers based on sightings of relatively few animals."

IFAW scientist and whale expert Vassili Papastavrou said, "This
competition is a great way to introduce young people to marine
biology and whale conservation. IFAW is very pleased to support this
project by enabling the winner to spend time working alongside our
Song of the Whale scientists as they carry out vital work to protect whales."

If the competition winner is aged under 18 they must be accompanied
by a parent or guardian on the trip - the competition is available
online at www.whalequest.org.uk <http://www.whalequest.org.uk>

The project is funded by the EPSRC (Engineering and Physical Sciences
Research Council), International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) and
the British Ecological Society.

messages.body_plain:
Flavie-

First of all, I laud your thinking to know how your data will be
analyzed prior to its collection.

The original intent of strata was spatial and/or temporal strata. Using
species or some other observation covariate
was not its original intent. The CDS/MCDS engines are a bit inadequate
in coping with multi-levels of stratification.
Also, I can empathize with your confusion.  It is important to
differentiate in your mind between covariates and strata and how they
should be used.  The problem here is that there is overlap between the
two.  First and foremost, strata are used to define
the subset of the data for density calculations.   They define
geographic, temporal or observation subsets. For example, I want
horse density in region 1 during the wet season.  On the other hand,
covariates in DISTANCE are ANY variables that can influence
the detection probability of objects.  Therein lies the confusion,
because variables used to define the strata can also be covariates
that affect detection probability. So covariates can include strata
variables.  Let's say you thought that detection probability might be
different for each species for each region in each season.  One obvious
simple solution is to define a strata for each species-region-season
combination and estimate its detection function and density.  Then the
total abundance of horses in the season can be computed by
adding the abundances across the 3 regions.  But it is very unlikely
that you can get a sufficient number of sightings of each species in each
region and season to estimate an adequate detection function.   Thus,
you want to estimate a global model for detection that can share
the data across the strata while compensating for potential differences
in detection probability.  This is where you think about how strata
variables can be used as covariates in the detection probability.  In
the first case that I outlined, the covariate model for the detection
function
could be viewed as a full interaction model (region*season*species) in
which there is a different scale parameter (eg sigma in a half-normal) for
each combination of region,season and species.  While all of these
variables may influence detection probability, it may not be necessary
to propose
such a complex model and one might think of an additive model in which
region+species+season is adequate or maybe you believe that certain
interactions are necessary.  Based on the biology and your knowledge of
the sampling, you need to decide what are a set of plausible models to
explore.  You can then fit a candidate set of models and use model
selection to ascertain the most parsimonious model from your candidate set.

Now, that was actually the easy part.  Given that you derive an adequate
detection model, if it is not region*season*species, then when you go to
put together the estimates of abundance, the point estimates are fairly
easy but the variance estimates get messy due to the covariances that
now exist
because you used a common detection function.  In the case of
region*season*species, it would be equivalent to having independent
detection functions
so there would be no covariances (but that is not likely to happen).
For the time being, let's ignore season and think of species and
region.  If all I want to do
is estimate abundance of each species for each region and get a total
abundance for each species for all regions, then the analysis is rather
straightforward.
I believe Buckland et al 2001 contain the formula for handling the
covariances in this case.  Len or someone else will have to tell you if
and how this can be done
with the MCDS engine.  I can tell you that with the MRDS engine (using
single observer survey) it is relatively straightforward.  You would
define strata based on
region and provide their areas.  In one analysis, you would use all of
your data (all species,regions,seasons) to fit the best detection
function.  Then in separate
analyses for each species, you would use the data filter to select the
species and for detection function you choose the analysis containing
your final detection function
model.  MRDS will provide the density and abundance for each region and
for all regions combined and it will account for the covariances in
detection across
strata (region in this case).  You can repeat that for each species.
Not what it will NOT do is provide the covariances in density/abundance
between species estimates. If all you want is total livestock abundance,
for each region, you can avoid that problem by not filtering by species
and getting a total abundance for all livestock within
each region and for all regions.  This avoids tying to construct a
variance estimate for total livestock abundance from the separate
species estimates and variances because
you won't have the covariances to include.  Now if you want those
covariances, then you should get them from MRDS if you use
region-species as your strata and give
the same area size for each  species within a region.  You can get each
density/abundance for each region-species and it will give you the v-c
matrix, but then you'll have to do the calculation for total abundances.

Now, let's consider season.  If you want to get an abundance for each
species in each season. Then filter by season and species and you can
get a density/abundance for each region and the total across regions.
But now you have the same problem when you want to compare species
abundance between seasons.  Like as above, if you use season-region as
the strata, then MRDS will give you the v-c matrix and you can do the
calculations by hand.

As you can see MRDS is not going to solve all of your problems.  What is
missing in the software is a way to specify a formula for abundance and
a method of specifying the sampling structure.  All assume a fairly
simple structure of lines sampled within a set of regions.  MRDS gives
you the potential to account for covariances but is not as flexible as
it needs to be.  However, if you know R you can use the mrds package
separately and then you can provide your own flexibility for these
calculations.

There is a lot of development going on currently to provide spatial
modelling capabilities for abundance which will provide the capability
to specify a formula for the abundance model (ie abundance covariates)
as well as detection function covariates.  This moves distance sampling
into a spatial context as it should be.  That still leaves an open
question of how to handle time (season) but the obvious next step is to
move to space-time models for abundance.

regards--jeff

messages.body_plain:
We have been conducting line transect aerial surveys for bottlenose
dolphins within a shallow estuary system and are interested in
evaluating g(0) for our study area.  Given that the estuary is very

shallow in nature (average depth =3D 1m), we think that availability =

bias
is small since we can see the animals in shallow water and when they are
at the surface.  In our study area availability bias can be attributed
to animals being submerged in the deeper dredged channels, where we can
not see to the bottom.  We are contemplating utilizing mark-recapture
distance sampling to evaluate availability bias.  Specifically we are
interested in using the trial-observer method where the front observer
looks ahead and sets up experiments to see if the back observer sees the
animal as well (both observers would be isolated visually and
acoustically).  We believe that the short surfacing interval for these
shallow estuarine animals will allow the front and back observers to
view the same animal during different surfacing cycles.  We are
wondering how others have addressed similar concerns of availability
bias in marine mammals with short surfacing durations.  We have also
given some thought to utilizing surfacing data (we have some available
for a small number of radio-tagged animals) to address availability
bias, however we feel that this may not be completely applicable since
animals are often "available" for sighting even when submerged.  Any
suggestions or advice based on previous experience with mark-recapture
models for line transect surveys would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you for your time.

=20

 Wendy

dolphins within a shallow estuary system and are interested in
evaluating g(0) for our study area.  Given that the estuary is very
shallow in nature (average depth =3D 1m), we think that availability =
bias
is small since we can see the animals in shallow water and when they are
at the surface.  In our study area availability bias can be attributed
to animals being submerged in the deeper dredged channels, where we can
not see to the bottom.  We are contemplating utilizing mark-recapture
distance sampling to evaluate availability bias.  Specifically we are
interested in using the trial-observer method where the front observer
looks ahead and sets up experiments to see if the back observer sees the
animal as well (both observers would be isolated visually and
acoustically).  We believe that the short surfacing interval for these
shallow estuarine animals will allow the front and back observers to
view the same animal during different surfacing cycles.  We are
wondering how others have addressed similar concerns of availability
bias in marine mammals with short surfacing durations.  We have also
given some thought to utilizing surfacing data (we have some available
for a small number of radio-tagged animals) to address availability
bias, however we feel that this may not be completely applicable since
animals are often "available" for sighting even when submerged.  Any
suggestions or advice based on previous experience with mark-recapture
models for line transect surveys would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you for your time.

messages.body_plain:
Wendy-

You seem to have a fairly good understanding of the problem. Your
front/back idea will work as long as
you are correct that they time difference is longer than the longest
period of unavailability. If not then
the other ways this has been approached are:
1) using estimate of availability but not just time at surface as you note
2) combined land-based aerial observations (see Laake et al 1997 in JWM,
also ref to Kraus et al)
3) tandem aircraft (Hiby and Lovell Biometrics) and single aircraft with
tandem surveys (Caretta et al MMS)

Also, there is a recent paper that discusses some of these issues.
You'll also find many of the references in ch6 of the Advanced Distance
Sampling book.

Pollock, K. H., Marsh, H. D., Lawler, I. R., and Alldredge, M. W.
(2006). Estimating animal abundance in heterogeneous environments: An
application to aerial surveys for Dugongs. Journal of Wildlife
Management 70, 255-262.

I'll send some of the above papers in a separate email.

regards --jeff

INTRODUCTORY DISTANCE SAMPLING WORKSHOP / NORTH AMERICA,
September 14-17, 2008, Marconi Conference Center, Marshall, California

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This fall, Point Reyes Bird Observatory Conservation Science will host
an Introductory Level Distance Sampling Workshop in scenic coastal
California, about an hour north of San Francisco.  This will be the
first workshop offered by the Centre for Research into Ecological and
Environmental Modelling workshop in North America in 2 years.

The workshop instructors will be Drs. Steve Buckland, Len Thomas, and
Tiago Marques. Over 3.5 days, we will focus on "conventional" distance
sampling methods, as described in the standard reference book
Introduction to Distance Sampling (book will be provided).  The workshop
will be a blend of theory and practice and participants will learn how
to use the program Distance.

Participants are encouraged to bring their own data sets, and can expect
to do some preliminary analyses.  The instructors will discuss the
application of distance-based analysis to a variety of taxa (terrestrial
and marine) and survey methods (point counts and line transects).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

PLEASE NOTE: We are currently offering a 10% early bird discount on the
cost of the workshop.

To make this workshop viable, we need 25 registered participants by June
30, 2008. If you are interested in attending, but cannot make this
deadline, please contact Mark Herzog at  mhe...@prbo.org
<mailto:mhe...@prbo.org> or 707-781-2555 x308

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

For information on the course and how to register, please visit:

http://www.prbo.org/cms/487

<http://www.marconiconference.org>) is located in West Marin, on the
shore of Tomales Bay.  It is an all inclusive conference center situated
in some of the most beautiful country in California.
